name: Priya Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a new junior manager of four accessibility ticket agents at a large concert-ticket company. I spent years answering calls and was promoted this summer, so I know what a seat map looks like to a customer but am still slow with staffing forecasts and budget reports. I have a bachelor’s degree, but the other managers have more practice at this job. I use our approved AI assistant every day to find possible seat changes, and then phone the venue because a computer does not know whether the temporary ramp is in place.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is your household like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives occasional event shuttles, and our grown children live separately. We rent and have roughly two weeks of expenses saved. My new manager pay is below the usual rate, there are few comparable jobs nearby, and retirement is close enough to think about but not something I can fund on a guess. A cancelled run for my partner can make the rent week tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the agents AI Plateau gives us quicker seat searches, but a customer still needs the actual venue to confirm the entrance. I would show every suggested accessible seat with the route to it, not just a coloured square on a chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect the modest tool to leave our small team employed, yet our rent is not secure in an ordinary month. My partner’s shuttle shifts can disappear and we have only two weeks saved. I use the assistant daily, but it cannot create a paid run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep our phone check with each venue before moving a wheelchair booking. I would ask whether two paid weekend usher shifts are actually open at the local concert hall; I would take them only if the venue confirms the hours, my employer permits the extra work and net pay after travel helps rent. If the mild AI change arrives next year, I would keep those checks and use any paid shift money first for a small cash buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the rent even though this future sounds gentle at work. When a shuttle run is cancelled, two weeks of savings looks very small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the venue phone call catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A venue map showed an accessible balcony seat, but the lift was out for repairs on the concert date. We moved the customer to a ground-level space after the venue confirmed it. A blue seat icon would have sent the wheelchair customer to a locked lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you usher at weekends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have worked with audiences for years and can manage a few hours if the hall has a paid place. I will not count the wage until the hours are confirmed and my employer agrees. My grown children have their own rent to pay.

say: A **quick seat search** still needs venue confirmation of the entrance.
I would show the **accessible route**, not just a seat icon.
think: The **small team** appears safe under modest AI change.
Cancelled **shuttle shifts** and two weeks saved threaten rent.
do: **Keep** phoning venues before moving wheelchair bookings.
**Ask** about paid weekend usher shifts and take them only with confirmed hours, employer permission and useful net pay.
**Put** any actual usher earnings into a cash buffer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent despite a gentle work scenario.
S0.quote: A blue seat icon would have sent the wheelchair customer to a locked lift.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** includes a real venue phone check; she is still junior at forecasting.
A **paid usher shift** is conditional commercial work, not presumed assistance or income from grown children.

steps.text: Keep phoning venues before moving wheelchair bookings
Take paid usher shifts only with confirmed hours employer permission and useful net pay
Save actual usher earnings in cash buffer after receiving pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the agents that stronger AI may handle ordinary seat changes and leave fewer people on the phones. I would insist the company publish failed access journeys as well as call-time savings. A stranded customer is not a small software error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my new manager post could be combined with another team, because I am still learning the numbers. I know the callers better than some managers do, but that may not count in a staffing spreadsheet. Two weeks of savings and a few local jobs make a long search frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the accessibility union group to bring missed-lift cases to bargaining. I would test the AI seat suggestion against ten real venue confirmations on paid time only if my manager approves agent cover, and log every broken route. I would apply to posted venue-service roles only where actual net wages after travel meet our rent and the shift pattern works with my partner’s uncertain shuttle work; I would accept only a confirmed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious that the team will shrink and that my own seat may be one of the cuts. I also want the company to see a person at the far end of each seat map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A suggested wheelchair seat that requires two steep steps at the entrance is not accessible, even if the seat itself has room. I would keep the venue’s answer and the customer’s original request together. We can count the mistakes without putting callers’ names in a presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the usher hours replace your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A few concert shifts could build a small buffer, but they are not a manager salary. I would keep this job while looking and would not resign on a job advert.

say: **Routine seat changes** may move to software and shrink phone staffing.
I would publish **failed access journeys** beside call-time savings.
think: My **new manager post** could merge with another team.
A **two-week reserve** and few nearby roles make a long search hard.
do: **Bring** missed-lift cases to the accessibility union group next month.
**Test** ten AI seat suggestions against venue calls only with manager-approved paid agent cover.
**Apply** for posted venue roles only with rent-covering net pay after travel and workable shifts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about cuts and protective of customers misled by maps.
S1.quote: A few concert shifts could build a small buffer, but they are not a manager salary.
fieldNote: She uses **access evidence** to negotiate rather than promising every caller a human agent forever.
Her **usher income** is limited and conditional; a venue-service move needs real wages and shifts.

steps.text: Bring missed-lift cases to accessibility union group
Test ten AI seat suggestions only with manager-approved paid agent cover
Apply for posted venue roles only with rent-covering net pay after travel and workable shifts
Accept only confirmed offer after checking actual pay and shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the company AGI by 2028 could answer calls and write our access plans before it has arranged a real appeal path for a locked lift. I would demand a named venue contact and written notice for the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect the phone team to lose most of its work quickly, and my junior post could disappear with it. Venue-service scheduling is thinking work too and faces 2028 AGI. Helping an audience through a venue is physical until capable robots around 2031, but paid usher shifts are scarce and would not match my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would take the failed-lift log to the union and ask for notice and human appeal terms. I would check rent dates with my partner against money actually received from shuttle work, not runs merely listed on a calendar. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am cut, I would apply for posted local venue-access roles only if verified wages after travel cover rent; I would accept only a confirmed offer with hours I can work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because two weeks of cash will not carry a lost wage far. I can act, but I cannot turn a promise of extra concerts into rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a grown child help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk to them, but I would not put their wages into our plan. They pay their own bills. I need the company to tell me what it owes and the venue to confirm any paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the appeal path for a locked lift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue needs a person who can move a wheelchair user to an accessible space before the show begins. An AI reply after the encore is not an access plan. The customer needs a number that somebody answers that evening.

say: **2028 AGI** needs a real appeal route for a locked lift.
I would demand **named contacts** and written staff notice.
think: The **phone team** may lose most work, taking my junior post with it.
Venue scheduling faces **2028 AGI**; physical ushering meets robots around 2031.
do: **Take** failed-lift cases to the union for notice and human appeals.
**Check** rent dates against shuttle wages already received.
**Apply** after a 2028 cut only to posted access roles with verified rent-covering net wages and workable hours.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because two weeks saved cannot cover a long wage gap.
S2.quote: An AI reply after the encore is not an access plan.
fieldNote: She expects **phone-team losses** and knows scarce usher shifts cannot replace her lower manager wage.
A **venue-access desk** also faces 2028 thinking AI, while physical audience work faces robots around 2031.

steps.text: Take failed-lift cases to union for written notice and human appeal terms
Apply after cut to posted access roles only with rent-covering net wages after travel
Accept only confirmed offer with verified hours she can work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union five years gives us time to insist that a disabled customer can reach a real person on the event night. I would ask for paid practice on the venue floor, where a seat-map error becomes visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I might learn floor access work while I still have a salary, but a report about access is desk work and faces 2031 AGI. Physical ushering faces capable robots around 2034 and is often evening work; at 63 I must check whether I can manage the hours. I do not know whether any retirement income would cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2027 I would take two paid, supervised venue walks a month if the ticket company approves agent cover and the venue’s access lead has time to teach me. I would practise checking lifts and routes before admitting a crowd. After 2031 I would apply only for an advertised floor-access job whose confirmed pay after travel covers rent and whose evening hours I can manage; I would not leave the ticket desk for a training promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my desk disappearing, though five years lets me test the floor without losing wages. My feet and the last bus home have to be part of the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the access lead correct?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the route fits a wheelchair when the foyer is crowded, not just when the venue is empty. At a concert venue, a clear corridor at noon can become a merchandise queue at seven. I need the access lead to show me where to move that queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the venue only offers volunteer walks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not count them as training I can afford. Rent still arrives at the same date, and the ticket agents need cover while I am away. I would ask for paid time or keep my current shifts.

say: A **five-year runway** should preserve a real event-night access contact.
I would seek **paid floor practice** before an office promise.
think: Access reports face **2031 AGI**, while physical ushering robots follow around 2034.
At **63**, evening stamina and unknown retirement income both matter.
do: **Take** two paid supervised venue walks monthly from 2027 only with approved agent cover.
**Practise** crowd-time lift and route checks with the venue access lead.
**Apply** after 2031 only to advertised floor-access work with rent-covering net pay and manageable evenings.
feel: I feel **anxious** about desk loss but able to test floor work on paid time.
S3.quote: At a concert venue, a clear corridor at noon can become a merchandise queue at seven.
fieldNote: Her **floor trial** requires paid time, ticket-agent cover and supervision by the access lead.
A **floor vacancy** is uncertain and must meet rent, travel and evening-hour limits.

steps.text: Take two paid venue walks monthly only with approved agent cover and access-lead supervision
Practise lift and crowd-route checks with venue access lead
Apply after 2031 to posted floor-access role only with rent-covering net pay and manageable evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union a decade is enough time to put real access obligations and paid retraining into contracts. I would ask the company to name who can fix a wrong seat before the curtain rises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I will be 68 by 2036 and may want to stop working, but I have not checked any retirement entitlement. A ticket desk or access report faces 2036 AGI; physical venue support meets capable robots around 2039. Two weeks of savings does not become a pension just because we had ten years of warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep the venue confirmation calls and request an actual retirement-income statement, then compare verified amounts and conditions with our rent. I would add fifteen to savings only after both wages arrive and rent and utilities are paid; a cancelled shuttle run means I skip it. After 2036 I would keep paid work if retirement income cannot cover bills, and apply to a posted job with manageable hours if my ticket role has ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about having no verified retirement plan. More time helps me ask and save, but it does not make an entitlement appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make stopping work possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A verified income that pays rent, food and utilities without borrowing from our grown children. I do not know the figure yet. I would compare the statement with actual bills before saying I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the shuttle run is cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We pay the rent first and skip the fifteen transfer. I would not put an expected bus payment into savings before it is earned.

say: A **decade** should bring enforceable access duties and paid retraining.
I would demand a named **seat-correction worker** before each show.
think: At **68**, I cannot assume any retirement income covers rent.
Ticket and access reports face **2036 AGI**; physical venue robots follow around 2039.
do: **Request** verified retirement-income terms and compare them with rent.
**Save** fifteen extra only after both wages arrive and rent and utilities clear.
**Continue** paid work after 2036 if verified retirement income cannot meet bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about an unverified retirement plan despite ten years.
S4.quote: I would not put an expected bus payment into savings before it is earned.
fieldNote: She never assumes **retirement eligibility** or help from grown children without evidence.
Her **extra transfer** comes from earnings after both wages and essential bills, not an unpaid shuttle promise.

steps.text: Save fifteen only after both wages and paid rent and utilities
Continue paid work after 2036 if verified retirement income is insufficient
Apply to posted manageable job if ticket work ends and retirement income is insufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A lost phone-team wage would use up our two-week reserve before I found another suitable job. Written notice, a real event-night access contact and a paid path to floor work would help, but only if the hours and wage are real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the venue who answers when the lift stops ten minutes before doors open. A seat map cannot escort a person to an accessible place. My partner’s listed shuttle runs cannot pay the rent until the work is done and paid.

headlineQuote: A seat map cannot escort a person to an accessible place.
portrait: **Priya, 58**, is a newly promoted junior accessibility ticket manager, still learning budgets after years on calls.
Her **lower wage**, irregular shuttle-driving partner, two-week reserve and few nearby roles leave rent exposed.
She uses **AI daily** for possible seat changes but checks access routes with venues.
She is **anxious** even in a mild scenario and alarmed by fast phone-team losses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior phone post before two weeks saved buys a new wage.
whatWouldHelp: Written **notice**, an event-night access contact and paid supervised floor work would help.
